Introduction
This collection presents the Universal Particle Law in its two complementary formulations,
together with the scale hierarchy that connects the proton to the galaxy and the human scale that
sits between them.
The Universal Particle Law begins from a simple proposal: what we experience as mass is not an
intrinsic property of matter but a resistance to the rotation of a particle's motion out of the
temporal dimension and into space. When we push on a particle, we are diverting some of its
motion through time into motion through space. The resistance to this rotation — inertia — is
quantified by a normal force that depends on Planck's constant, the speed of light, and a
fundamental timescale. Remarkably, when the law is applied to the proton, the neutron, and the
electron, the same timescale emerges: approximately one second.
The first paper in this collection develops the law in two equivalent forms. In one, the normal
force is written in terms of Planck's constant, and the mass of a particle is generated by that force
acting over the particle's cross-sectional area, mediated by the pliability of space as measured by
Newton's constant. This formulation makes the geometric picture of inertia explicit: mass is the
resistance of an extended area to the rotation of temporal velocity into spatial velocity. In the
other formulation, the same law is written in terms of the reduced Planck constant, and it takes a
form directly analogous to the Bohr ground state of hydrogen. The celestial effective action for
the Earth–Moon–Sun system is derived from this analogy, using the accurately known mass of
the Moon as its anchor. Both formulations return the same one-second invariant. They differ only
in which aspect of the physics they emphasize.
The second paper presents the original formulation of the law and its first extension beyond the
particle scale. It shows that the same one-second resonance appears in the Earth–Moon–Sun
system — where the geometric coupling is the ratio of the Moon's orbital radius to the Sun's
radius, the condition for a near-perfect solar eclipse — and in the Sun's orbit around the galactic
center, where two additional resonant nodes appear: the asteroid belt at roughly 2.4 astronomical
units, and the orbit of Saturn at roughly 9.5. These are not independent coincidences. They are
resonant nodes of the same law, fixed by the Sun's mass, radius, and motion through the galaxy.
The third paper identifies the human scale as the middle rung of this hierarchy. The human
effective action is the geometric mean of the Planck constant and the celestial effective action,
and the human energy scale that follows is on the order of the mechanical work of a heartbeat.
The geometric means of particle and astrophysical masses bracket the human mass range, from a
few grams to several tens of kilograms. The human scale is not an arbitrary biological fact; it is
the resonant node between the quantum and the astrophysical.
An appendix provides a careful treatment of the twenty-four-hour day as a stable resonance
plateau. The Earth–Moon–Sun system is dynamically locked near a flat extremum of the
resonance function: the Moon's recession and Earth's rotational slowdown are coupled so as to
of 4 56
keep the resonance product nearly constant over geological time. The observed day length lies
inside a predicted window of stability, and the plateau has persisted for hundreds of millions of
years — long enough for complex life to emerge.
Two further appendices, included in the broader collection but not reproduced here in full,
examine the relationship between the Universal Particle Law and two independent theoretical
programs: a five-dimensional metric-affine reduction proposed by Chiaramonte and collaborators
within the ANKHOR research group, and the Quantum Relativity framework of Bermanseder. In
both cases the honest assessment is structural complementarity rather than derivation. The
Universal Particle Law supplies an empirical convergence across scales that neither framework
generates on its own; those frameworks supply candidate algebraic foundations for the form of
the force law. The relationship is best described as two views of a common structure, each
awaiting the other's completion.
The thread that runs through all of these papers is the one-second resonance. It appears in the
proton, the neutron, and the electron. It appears in the Earth–Moon–Sun system and in the Sun's
orbit around the galaxy. It appears at the human scale, as the mechanical work of a heartbeat. The
universe, on this account, is resonant — and we are not merely observers of that resonance but
its expression at the human scale.
The work is presented in the tradition of phenomenological laws awaiting deeper algebraic
derivation. The normal force can be derived from the Principle of Least Action, and the one-
second invariant has the character of a structural fact rather than a numerical accident. But the
value of the second is not derived from first principles; it is read from particle data. What the law
does is show that the same characteristic time governs bound systems across more than forty
orders of magnitude in mass and radius, and that the couplings which appear in the law are not
free parameters but are determined by the geometry and internal structure of the systems they
describe.
The papers are collected here in the order in which they develop the framework: two
formulations of the law, the celestial extension, the human scale, and the dynamical stability of
the twenty-four-hour plateau. Read together, they present a single, testable proposal: that the
structure of bound systems throughout the universe is governed by a one-second invariant, and
that the human scale is where that invariant becomes visible to itself.

Abstract
The Universal Particle Law (UPL) admits two mathematically equivalent formulations. In the
-formulation, the normal force acts on a particle's cross-sectional area to
generate mass, making explicit the geometric picture of inertia as resistance to the rotation of
temporal velocity into space. In the -formulation, the same law takes a form directly analogous
to the Bohr ground state of hydrogen, with the Moon's mass playing the role of the electron's
charge and the gravitational constant replacing the Coulomb constant. This yields a celestial
effective action J·s, derived from and numerically close to .
The energy–action law unifies the scales from the proton to the galaxy. The
human scale emerges as the geometric mean , giving J in the
-formulation and J in the -formulation—both on the order of the mechanical work of a
heartbeat. The relation between and the Planck force is an exact algebraic identity arising
from the convention; it does not fix the one-second value, which comes from particle data.
We argue that both formulations are physically meaningful and complementary, and we identify
open questions for future work.
1. Introduction
The Universal Particle Law (UPL) identifies a one-second invariant across scales [1]. The law
can be written in two equivalent ways. The first uses Planck's constant :
The second uses the reduced Planck constant . The two formulations are
algebraically equivalent, but they emphasize different aspects of the physics. The -formulation
makes explicit the interaction of the normal force with the particle's cross-sectional area
, which is the geometric core of the inertia mechanism. The -formulation reveals a
direct analogy with the Bohr ground state of hydrogen and leads to a natural definition of
celestial effective actions.

At the particle scale, is the energy of a photon with angular frequency
rad/s. Its ordinary frequency is Hz, and its wavelength is
This is a numerical curiosity: the wavelength of the "1 rad/s photon" is about times the solar

that the particle-scale energy is exactly per second—the reduced Planck constant is the energy
quantum of the one-radian-per-second mode.

1. Derivation of . The Bohr analog gives a precise value for , but it is a guess about the
form of the celestial quantum. Can be derived from the Moon's mass and the one-second
invariant without the Bohr analog as an input? A derivation from first principles would be
stronger.
2. The galactic scale. The galactic effective action is defined by the Sun's
kinetic energy. Is there a Bohr-like equation for the galaxy, or is the galactic scale defined only
by the energy–action law? The Earth scale has a Bohr analog; the galactic scale does not, at least
not obviously.
3. The 6% difference. The difference between and is about 6%. Is this physically
significant, or is it due to the choice of average versus perihelion velocity? A careful treatment of
the Earth's orbital velocity would settle this.
4. The relation. The algebraic identity is exact, but it might be a shadow of a deeper
geometric fact about the rotation of temporal velocity into space. Is there a dynamical
interpretation of the that survives the convention?
5. The heartbeat. The human energy scale J (in the -formulation) is on the
order of a heartbeat. Can this be connected to a specific biological mechanism, or is it a
numerical coincidence?
6. The 1 rad/s photon. The wavelength of the 1 rad/s photon is about . Is this structural, or is
it a numerical curiosity?
9. Conclusion
The Universal Particle Law admits two equivalent formulations. The -formulation emphasizes
the geometric picture of inertia as a force acting over a cross-section. The -formulation
emphasizes the Bohr-like structure of celestial scales and leads to the energy–action law
. Both formulations give the same one-second invariant, and both are
physically meaningful.
The celestial effective action is anchored by the Bohr analog s, which uses
the accurately known Moon mass and gives J·s. The energy–action law
extends this to the galaxy and to the human scale, where the geometric mean
gives J in the -formulation—on the order of a heartbeat.
The relation between and the Planck force is exact but conventional. It does not fix the
one-second value, which comes from particle data. Both formulations are correct; the choice
between them should be guided by the aspect of the resonance one wishes to emphasize.

Abstract
We present a universal particle law (UPL) where what we experience as mass is taken as
resistance to changes in a particle’s motion through the temporal dimension to the spacial when
pushed on, which is measured by G, the universal constant of gravitation. To do this we
introduce a normal force given by where is on the order of second, which
is Lorentz invariant. The normal force, is exposed to the cross-sectional area of the particle
. The result is the mass of the particle is given by , with experimental
verification giving 1.00500 seconds (proton), 1.00803 seconds (neutron), and 0.99773 seconds
(electron). The coupling constant, ,, is suggest by a prediction for the radius of the proton,
which is with where is the golden ratio, and in
general is predicted by the fact that for the electron, with no substructure, it has its equal to 1,
meaning it matches the analytic structure of a force subjected to a cross-sectional area, directly.
We derive the normal force from the Lagrangian.
We further find we can produce a quantum analog for our planetary system (PSQA) and show
that there is scale invariance from quantum scales to celestial scales (SIQC) in the Universal
Particle Equation (UPL).

The Moon allows for the evolution of complex, intelligent life because it stabilizes the earth tilt
to its orbit allowing for the seasons and preventing temperature extremes. We live in an
interesting time when the Moon near perfectly eclipses the Sun. This is because while the Sun is
400 times larger than the Moon, it is 400 times further from the Earth than the Moon is. That is
the perfect eclipse is given by the orbital radius of the Earth to the Moon’s orbital radius
equals the Solar radius to the lunar radius :
The Earth's rotation is slowing down, and as a direct result, the Moon is slowly drifting away.
Earth's Rotation Slowing: The length of a day is increasing by about 2.3 milliseconds per
century. This is the long-term average rate caused primarily by the Moon's tidal pull. (Note that
this rate can be influenced by other factors; for example, climate change is currently contributing
about 1.33 milliseconds per century).
Moon's Orbit Growing: The Moon is receding from Earth at a rate of about 3.8 centimeters (1.5
inches) per year.
The Tidal Connection
These two phenomena are linked by tidal friction. The Moon's gravity creates tides in Earth's
oceans. As Earth rotates, the tidal bulges are pulled slightly ahead of the Moon, creating friction
that slows Earth's spin.
To conserve angular momentum in the Earth-Moon system, this loss of Earth's rotational speed is
transferred to the Moon, boosting its orbital energy and causing it to spiral outward into a larger
orbit. This recession rate has been precisely measured for decades using the Lunar Laser Ranging
experiment, which bounces lasers off reflectors left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts.
Long-Term Perspective
While these changes are tiny on human timescales, they have significant effects over millions of
years. About 250 million years ago, a day on Earth was roughly 23 hours long. In about 600
million years, the Moon will have drifted so far that total solar eclipses will no longer be
possible.

The Human Scale as a Resonant Node Between the Quantum and
Astrophysical Scales
Ian Beardsley
September 30, 2026
Abstract
We propose that the human scale — the characteristic mass, length, and energy of biological
organisms — is not an arbitrary biological fact but a resonant node between the quantum scale
and the Earth–Moon–Sun scale. Using the Universal Particle Law (UPL), which posits a one-
second resonance governing bound systems from the proton to the galaxy, we construct a human
effective action , where is Planck's constant and is the
Earth–Moon–Sun effective action. With the UPL's one-second timescale, this gives a human
energy scale — on the order of the mechanical work of a heartbeat — and a
characteristic length-to-mass ratio (for ). The geometric means of
particle masses and astrophysical masses bracket the human mass range: ,
, , and . Extending the cascade to the
galactic scale, we identify two additional resonant nodes — the asteroid belt at ~2.4 AU and
Saturn at ~9.5 AU — that complete a scale hierarchy to . We suggest this
hierarchy provides a quantitative framework for astrobiology: the conditions for human-scale
intelligence may be geometrically fixed, and the search for life should target systems with the
same resonant architecture.

4. Human-Scale Masses from Geometric Means
The geometric means of particle masses and astrophysical masses bracket the human mass range:
Geometric Mean Masses!
The proton–Earth and proton–Sun geometric means are exactly human-scale masses. The
electron–Earth and electron–Sun means are also human-scale, though smaller. The human body
sits at the geometric midpoint between the quantum and astrophysical scales.
This is a striking quantitative result: the human mass range is the geometric mean of the quantum
and astrophysical mass scales.

6. Astrobiology Implications
6.1 The resonant architecture
If the human scale is a resonant node between the quantum and astrophysical scales, and if the
Earth–Moon–Sun system is tuned to produce this node, then life requires a planetary system with
specific architectural features:
1. A rocky planet at ~1 AU — where liquid water is stable.
2. An asteroid belt at ~2.4 AU — to deliver water and organics.
3. A gas giant at ~9.5 AU — to shield the inner system.
4. A large moon — to stabilize obliquity and produce a ~24-hour day.
5. A perfect eclipse geometry — , the eclipse ratio.
The UPL predicts these from the Sun's mass, radius, and galactic motion. They are not
independent coincidences; they are resonant nodes of the same one-second law.
6.2 The search strategy
The astrobiology prediction is specific and falsifiable:
Look for exoplanetary systems with an asteroid belt at ~2.4 AU and a gas giant at ~9.5 AU.
These are the systems where the human-scale resonance can emerge.

geometrically fixed. This gives us a concrete target for astrobiology.

The Earth's rotation is slowing down, and as a direct result, the Moon is slowly drifting away.
Earth's Rotation Slowing: The length of a day is increasing by about 2.3 milliseconds per
century. This is the long-term average rate caused primarily by the Moon's tidal pull. (Note that
this rate can be influenced by other factors; for example, climate change is currently contributing
about 1.33 milliseconds per century).
Moon's Orbit Growing: The Moon is receding from Earth at a rate of about 3.8 centimeters (1.5
inches) per year.

The Tidal Connection
These two phenomena are linked by tidal friction. The Moon's gravity creates tides in Earth's
oceans. As Earth rotates, the tidal bulges are pulled slightly ahead of the Moon, creating friction
that slows Earth's spin.
To conserve angular momentum in the Earth-Moon system, this loss of Earth's rotational speed is
transferred to the Moon, boosting its orbital energy and causing it to spiral outward into a larger
orbit. This recession rate has been precisely measured for decades using the Lunar Laser Ranging
experiment, which bounces lasers off reflectors left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts.
Long-Term Perspective
While these changes are tiny on human timescales, they have significant effects over millions of
years. About 250 million years ago, a day on Earth was roughly 23 hours long. In about 600
million years, the Moon will have drifted so far that total solar eclipses will no longer be
possible.

7.4 Testability
The framework makes specific predictions:
- The UPL should hold at the human scale with and .
- Exoplanetary systems with an asteroid belt at ~2.4 AU and a gas giant at ~9.5 AU should be
more likely to host complex life.
- Systems without these features should be less likely to host complex life.
These predictions are testable with current and future data.
8. Conclusion
We have shown that the human scale emerges as a resonant node between the quantum scale and
the Earth–Moon–Sun scale. The human effective action is the geometric mean of the Planck
constant and the celestial effective action:
With the UPL's one-second resonance, this gives a human energy scale and a
characteristic length-to-mass ratio . The geometric means of particle and
astrophysical masses bracket the human mass range. Extending the cascade to the galactic scale,
we identify the asteroid belt and Saturn as additional resonant nodes.
The human scale is not an arbitrary biological fact. It is the middle rung of a scale hierarchy that
spans from the proton to the galaxy. This suggests a quantitative framework for astrobiology: the
conditions for human-scale intelligence may be geometrically fixed, and the search for life
should target systems with the same resonant architecture.

Appendix: Dimensionless Reformulation of the UPL Hierarchy
A.1 Motivation
A natural objection to the Universal Particle Law (UPL) is that its central result, second,
appears to depend on the human convention of the second. The second, kilogram, meter, and
joule are human units. If the UPL describes a structural resonance, its significance should survive
the removal of human measurement conventions.
This appendix addresses that objection directly. We reformulate the UPL in an -normalized
natural unit system, show that the law collapses to a pure ratio statement, and demonstrate that
the full hierarchy — electron, proton, neutron, Earth–Moon–Sun, human, galaxy — converges to
a single dimensionless coordinate. The resonance survives the removal of SI units.

The dimensionless reformulation does not derive the value from first principles. It
